title: Why Is the Sky Blue? The Real Science of a Blue Sky
hook: Sunlight is white. Space is black. And yet, every clear day, the sky above you glows blue. Where does all that blue actually come from?
notes: Curated long-form sample (science identity). Sources: Wikipedia 'Diffuse sky radiation', 'Rayleigh scattering', 'Twilight'. Numbers used: about 23 percent of direct sunlight scattered; Leonardo da Vinci c. 1506-1510; John Tyndall 1869; Lord Rayleigh 1871; twilight ends when the Sun is 18 degrees below the horizon. Leonardo's idea is presented as a conjecture.

beats.narration: Sunlight is white. Space is black. And yet, every clear day, the sky above you glows blue. Where does all that blue actually come from?
Think about the last time you lay on the grass and looked up. That deep, endless blue feels so normal that most of us never question it.
But the sky isn't painted blue. The air you breathe looks perfectly clear in a glass. So how can a clear gas turn an entire sky blue?

visual.title: How does clear air look blue?

beats.narration: And while we're at it, why are sunsets orange and red instead? And why are clouds white? It turns out all three questions share one beautiful answer.
Let's start with sunlight itself. It looks white, but it's really a mixture of every color of the rainbow, all traveling together.
You can see this for yourself with a glass prism. Shine white light through it, and the colors fan out into a rainbow, from red on one side to violet on the other.
Each color is a wave of light, and the colors differ in one important way: their wavelength. Red light has long, lazy waves. Blue light has short, tightly packed waves.
Remember that difference, because it's about to matter a lot.
Above you sits a thin blanket of air called the atmosphere. Most of it is nitrogen, with some oxygen, made of molecules far too small to see.
These molecules are much smaller than the wavelength of light. And when light meets particles that tiny, something special happens: the light gets scattered, bounced off in new directions.
Here's the key. Shorter wavelengths are scattered far more strongly than longer ones. So blue light gets bounced around the sky, while red light mostly carries straight on.
And it's not a small effect. About 23 percent of direct sunlight is scattered out of the beam like this, filling the whole sky with light.
That's why the sky glows even in places where the Sun isn't. Look away from the Sun, and the light reaching your eyes is mostly this scattered blue, arriving from every direction.
In other words, the blue sky is sunlight that has been sorted. The air pulls the blue out of the beam and spreads it across the sky above you.
So who figured this out? The story takes centuries, and it starts with a famous painter.
Around 1506 to 1510, Leonardo da Vinci suggested that sunlight scattering off tiny particles in the air might give the sky its blue color. It was a remarkable guess.
In 1869, the physicist John Tyndall noticed that bright light scattering off extremely tiny particles took on a bluish tint. The idea was getting closer.
Then in 1871, Lord Rayleigh worked out the math. He showed exactly why tiny molecules scatter short blue wavelengths so much more than long red ones. Today we call it Rayleigh scattering.
His paper set up the basic scientific model for the color of the sky, and it's still the explanation scientists use today.
Now for the plot twist. If air scatters blue light so well, why does the sky turn orange and red at sunset?
At noon, sunlight takes a short trip straight down through the air. But when the Sun is low, its light has to cross a much longer stretch of atmosphere to reach you.
Along that long path, most of the blue gets scattered away before it ever arrives. What's left is the light that scatters least: yellow, orange and red.
As the Sun sinks lower, the sky keeps dimming. When the Sun is 18 degrees below the horizon, the light from the sky is nearly zero and twilight becomes night.
And clouds? Their water droplets are much bigger than the wavelength of light, so they scatter all colors about equally. Mix every color together, and you get white.
On a fully overcast day there's no direct sunlight at all. Every bit of light you see has been scattered through the clouds, which is why it looks so soft and gray.
But wait. Violet waves are even shorter than blue ones. So shouldn't the sky be violet?
The scattered light really does contain both blue and violet, coming from all over the sky. But your eyes respond to that mix as if it were blue mixed with white.
That's why the sky looks a soft, pale blue rather than a deep, saturated violet. The color you see depends on the light and on the eyes doing the seeing.
So let's put it all together. Sunlight is a mix of colors. Tiny air molecules scatter the short blue waves across the sky. Long red waves travel on.
At sunset the long path strips the blue away, leaving reds and oranges. And big cloud droplets scatter everything, so clouds look white.
So the next time you look up at a blue sky, remember: you're seeing sunlight that the air has sorted, just for you. Stay curious!
